description: We're Team SARtorial. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we've gathered a group of remarkable people with experts in software development, research, earth science and astrophysics alike. With our desire to tackle real world challenges with intuitive application, we hope to have an amazing journey this year.
summary:
SARsight turns NASA–ISRO NISAR radar data into plain answers that ordinary people can act on. NISAR can see floods through cloud and measure ground sinking by the centimeter, but almost no farmer or family can read it.

SARsight has three modules:
- EconAssist is for farmers, fishers and mine workers. Pick your work, tap your field, and get one colour, one sentence and two pictures. It works in English and Bangla and reads its advice aloud.
- HazAssist is for residents. Draw any area and see its flood, ground-motion and landslide risk, plus live natural events nearby from NASA EONET.
- VisAssist is for scientists and researchers: a 4D globe with every layer, a 12-day time slider, swipe comparison and profiles.

Every layer is a real measurement and nothing is simulated. We use NISAR L-band scans and ground motion, Sentinel-1 radar every 12 days, NASA POWER rain and soil wetness, and more. Any place on Earth can be prepared on demand in about a minute.

It matters because the people most exposed to floods, subsidence and crop loss are the least able to use the satellites that already watch them.
details:
What it does

NISAR sees through cloud, day and night, which matters most in monsoon countries like Bangladesh. The data is hard to use: raw files run to gigabytes, values come in decibels and radar phase, and the processing takes expert software. SARsight does that work and hands people a decision.

- EconAssist (livelihoods): the user picks their work (farmer, fisher, miner, oil worker) and taps their field. They get one status (OK, Watch or Alert, shown with both a colour and a symbol), one plain sentence such as "Too much water in the field. Open the drains.", and two simple pictures. It works in Bangla and English, reads advice aloud, and uses large touch targets for people with limited reading skills.

- HazAssist (residents): answers "Is my home safe, and what should I do?" A polygon tool lets anyone draw an area and get a plain-language risk card covering flooding, ground sinking, landslides and earthquakes. It also lists live natural events within 300 km from NASA EONET.

- VisAssist (researchers): a full 4D globe with every layer, a 12-day time slider across up to 30 consecutive passes, swipe comparison, profiles, and full source credits.

How it works

- Ready places: a Python pipeline fetches real observations along with 10 prefetched showcase places in Bangladesh, Pakistan, Türkiye, Italy and Mexico, on a common grid:

- NISAR L-band GCOV backscatter for 9 places.

- NISAR GUNW interferograms chained into a cumulative ground-motion series (Mexico City, Campi Flegrei).

- Sentinel-1 radar on strict 12-day repeat passes.

- COMET LiCSAR interferograms for ground motion.

- NASA POWER rain and soil moisture.

- Elevation, land cover, 38 years of water history, and earthquakes.

- Plain-language rules: analysis code turns these layers into indicators, such as flood extent from radar backscatter, soil wetness, crop growth, and ground velocity. Plain-language rules then turn the indicators into advice.

- On-demand places: a FastAPI backend builds any new place in about a minute, then adds the latest NISAR scan in the background.

- Offline-friendly: layers ship at half precision, so the app loads fast on phones and works without live APIs during a demo.

Tools

- Frontend: TypeScript, Next.js 15, React 19, three.js with React Three Fiber, d3-geo.

- Backend and pipeline: Python with FastAPI, NumPy, rasterio, h5py, earthaccess, pystac-client and shapely.

- Deployment: Docker and Caddy for the backend, Vercel for the frontend.

What makes it creative

One radar archive serves three very different people, each at their own level: one sentence for a farmer, a risk card for a family, the full data for a scientist. The same NISAR measurement becomes "open the drains" or a centimeter-scale motion map, depending on who is asking.

What we considered

- Honesty: every layer is a real measurement with a named source. We never present derived values as more than they are.

- Literacy and language: English & Bangla both, read-aloud, very little text.

- Accessibility: status is never shown by color alone, touch targets are at least 44 px, and every layout works on a 400 px-wide phone.

- Free data only: everything except NISAR science data needs no login.

- Speed: places open in about a minute.

Intended impact

Earlier action on floods and field drainage, safer decisions about where to live and build, and a path for NISAR's open data to reach the people it can help most. We started from Rajshahi, Bangladesh, and the same tool works for any place on Earth.
